title: Observer Pattern
oneLiner: Lets an object broadcast state changes to any number of subscribers, without knowing who they are.

hero.name: Signal-Man
hero.catchphrase: Subscribe once. I'll handle the rest!
hero.power: Broadcasts a single event to every subscriber instantly, without the sender knowing who's listening.
hero.weakness: Too many silent subscribers and nobody can trace who reacts to what — Signal-Man's signals can become impossible to follow.
hero.origin: Signal-Man emerged from a dashboard where the OrderService had to manually call sendEmail(), updateInventory(), and logAnalytics() by name every time an order shipped — and forgetting one caused real bugs.

story.problem: OrderService directly calls EmailService, InventoryService, and AnalyticsService every time an order ships. Add a new subscriber, and OrderService's code has to change too.
story.solution: Signal-Man lets OrderService just broadcast 'order shipped' — every subscriber that cares can listen in, and OrderService never needs to know they exist.
story.result: New subscribers plug in independently. OrderService stays focused on orders, not on notifying every downstream system by name.

before: OrderService calls every listener by name
OrderService knows too much about unrelated systems
after: OrderService only knows about a generic listener list
OrderService stays focused purely on shipping orders

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: OrderService calls three unrelated services directly, by name, every time an order ships.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Marketing wants a Slack notification on every shipment now. That means editing OrderService again — the fourth time this quarter.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: Signal-Man appears in a burst of static, antenna crackling.
panels.speaker: Signal-Man
panels.dialogue: Stop calling every listener by name. Just broadcast the event — subscribe once, and I'll handle the rest.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: OrderService becomes a Subject. Email, Inventory, Analytics, and now Slack all register as Observers.
panels.speaker: Signal-Man
panels.dialogue: You publish 'orderShipped'. Every subscriber picks it up on their own. You don't even know their names anymore — and you don't need to.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: The Slack notifier subscribes on its own. OrderService.ts doesn't change at all.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: I added the Slack notifier as a subscriber and didn't touch OrderService once. Marketing's happy, I'm relieved.

useWhen: One object's state change needs to trigger reactions in an open-ended, growing set of other objects.
You want to decouple the source of an event from the code that reacts to it.
The set of subscribers should be able to change at runtime without modifying the publisher.
avoidWhen: There's exactly one fixed listener — a direct method call is simpler and easier to trace.
Update ordering between subscribers matters a lot and needs to be strict; implicit broadcast order can be fragile.
The chain of notifications could cascade unpredictably (an observer's reaction triggers another notification, and so on) without any way to reason about the depth.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to unsubscribe, causing memory leaks and 'zombie' listeners that fire on stale objects.
Letting observers throw exceptions that break the publisher's loop, so one broken subscriber silently blocks the rest.
Overusing pub/sub for simple, direct call flows — it can obscure control flow if applied where a plain function call would be clearer.
Not documenting what event payloads look like, leaving subscribers guessing about shape and forcing brittle assumptions.
explanation.realWorldExample: DOM event listeners (`addEventListener`), React's state subscriptions, RxJS observables, and pub/sub message queues (like Redis Pub/Sub or Kafka topics) are all real-world Observer implementations.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: So OrderService has no idea who's subscribed?

conversation.speaker: Signal-Man
conversation.message: None. It just broadcasts. Every observer decides for itself whether to react — I'm just the signal in between.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: What happens if fifty things subscribe and nobody remembers why?

conversation.speaker: Signal-Man
conversation.message: That's my weakness — untracked subscribers make the system hard to trace. Keep your event names and payloads well documented, or my signals turn into noise.

codeBattle.scenario: Your stock-trading dashboard needs to update five different UI widgets the instant a price ticks, and new widgets get added by other teams every sprint.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: Signal-Man lets the price feed broadcast 'price changed' once, and any widget — current or future — can subscribe without the feed knowing they exist.

quiz.question: What relationship does the Observer pattern formalize?
options: A one-to-many dependency where one subject notifies many observers of state changes
A one-to-one relationship between two tightly coupled classes
A hierarchy where a base class is extended by many subclasses
A pooling mechanism that reuses expensive objects
quiz.answer: A one-to-many dependency where one subject notifies many observers of state changes
quiz.explanation: One subject, many observers — that fan-out notification is the defining shape of the pattern.

quiz.question: Why does Observer reduce coupling compared to calling each listener by name?
options: The subject only depends on a generic subscription interface, not on the concrete listener classes
It removes the need for any function calls at all
It guarantees listeners run in a fixed, documented order
It merges the subject and all its listeners into a single class
quiz.answer: The subject only depends on a generic subscription interface, not on the concrete listener classes
quiz.explanation: The subject just calls 'notify' on whatever is subscribed — it never imports or names the concrete listener classes.

quiz.question: What's a classic bug caused by misusing Observer?
options: Forgetting to unsubscribe a listener, causing a memory leak or updates to a stale/removed object
The subject running out of memory because it stores too many method names
Observers being unable to read the subject's public properties
TypeScript refusing to compile classes with subscribe() methods
quiz.answer: Forgetting to unsubscribe a listener, causing a memory leak or updates to a stale/removed object
quiz.explanation: Dangling subscriptions are one of the most common real-world Observer bugs, especially in long-lived UI components.

quiz.question: When might Observer be the wrong choice?
options: When there's exactly one fixed listener and a direct call would be simpler and easier to trace
When more than one object needs to react to an event
When the set of listeners might grow over time
When you want to decouple a publisher from its subscribers
quiz.answer: When there's exactly one fixed listener and a direct call would be simpler and easier to trace
quiz.explanation: Observer's value comes from decoupling a growing, dynamic set of listeners — with just one fixed listener, the indirection isn't worth it.
